Regarding the question about computational accuracy, we have organized our response into
Three parts to systematically address your concerns:
Fluorescence-to-Output Signal Conversion
The conversion of fluorescence signals to quantitative outputs is achieved through a pre-
calibrated standard curve. For each weighted calculation experiment, at least three standard
input/weight combinations (spanning the expected summation range) are processed under
identical reaction conditions as the experimental groups. A scatter plot is generated by assigning
the weighted summation values to the x-axis and the corresponding fluorescence intensities to
the y-axis. The standard curve is then derived from linear regression of these data points. This
approach ensures traceable and reproducible quantification, even for non-saturating
fluorescence signals. The specific fitting curve and R2 value are presented in
both the main text and supplementary information.
Mitigation of Accuracy Limitations
Regarding how our design achieves high computational accuracy and stability, we have
provided a systematic explanation in Figure 2 of the main text. Below we offer additional
clarifications and further elaboration.
We acknowledge potential confounding factors such as initial strand concentrations, pipetting
variability, and secondary structure interference. To address these:
Optimize DNA sequence design: We employed NUPACK to comprehensively predict and
eliminate potential secondary structures and crosstalk arising from DNA sequence design.
Moreover, both the strand length and CG content of each specific domain are fixed, ensuring
reaction parallelism and relatively uniform reaction kinetics.
Standardized Protocols: Stringent procedures for strand dissolution, concentration
measurement, dilution, and pipetting were implemented to minimize potential errors arising from
human factors in DNA concentration quantification and sample loading.
Thermal annealing procedure: As illustrated in Figure 2 and Figure R1, The allosteric toehold
strand displacement reaction is thermodynamically irreversible. This means that after sufficient
reaction with the corresponding substrate, the products will remain in a stable state rather than
a relatively unstable chemical equilibrium state. Building upon this principle, the thermal
annealing process directly helps the reaction overcome kinetic barriers, enabling uniform and
stable DNA strand binding while efficiently driving the system toward its stable state. This
protocol ensures consistent reaction kinetics and high computational fidelity. For further
validation, we have included control experiments without thermal annealing in Figure R4. Under
identical sample loading and detection conditions, the Figure R4B group subjected to thermal
annealing procedure demonstrated significantly improved reaction kinetics, better parallel
reproducibility, and faster plateau attainment compared to Figure R4A group, confirming
complete reaction progression.
Additional error-mitigation strategies are detailed in: (1) our interpretation of Figure 2 in the
response to Q3a, and (2) the rationale for selecting the T-strand as the output strand in our
response to Q14.

Q3: Relation between what is claimed and what is presented.
The authors make a number of claims in the paper that are not necessarily justified by the results
- or at least, not without being substantially more precise about the claims.
Q3a. positioning relative to the literature is somewhat imprecise. We think there is certainly
novelty within the system proposed, but it needs to be stated more accurately. The authors
describe their system as the first "fully analogue" DNA neural network, but then go on to describe
the system of Genot et al, which is also analog. They criticise aspects of this work, but then they
need to be careful about how they position their work with respect to it.
Response: Thank you for your question, which gave us the opportunity to further improve the
argument in the article. We would like to clarify and elaborate on the refined and innovative
design of the CALCUL unit's molecular structure. All of these design choices were specifically
implemented to achieve unprecedented analog computation precision. Additionally, these
features inadvertently distinguish our CALCUL unit from previously reported weighted
summation tools. We have summarized these design elements in Main text Figure 2.
Figure 2. Schematic illustration of the sources of the unprecedented computational
accuracy of the simulation of the CALCUL unit
The most fundamental point is the highly concise and thermodynamically homogeneous design
of our effective and null reaction paths. In a CALCUL cell, all P and Q-strands will enter the
same pair of gates/null gates. Regardless of the number of inputs and weights in the weighted
summation process, there is always only one gate/null gate, which makes our CALCUL cell
the most concise DNA tool for weighted summation. This simplicity brings two significant
benefits to computational accuracy: First, crosstalk between DNA strands greatly affects the
accuracy of analog computations; the fewer strands in the system, the less crosstalk there is,
which improves computational accuracy. Second, accurate weighted summation operations
require that the reaction thermodynamics of each additive (i.e., the input strand) be highly
approximate. In our CALCUL cell, all inputs assume the same strand substitution path; thus,
their reaction thermodynamics are identical, which greatly contributes to the computational
accuracy.
In addition to simplicity, another important molecular design is the thermodynamically identical
null gate. In the CALCUL unit, whether cis or trans, the thermodynamics of forming the PQT
triplex (the effective pathway) is absolutely equal to the thermodynamics of forming the P'QT
triplex (the null pathway); therefore, the weighting values will be very
accurate. It is worth noting that in the Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. paper1 , they designed only empty
weight strands (called matrix strands in their paper) but no empty gates (called reporters in their
paper), so the empty paths are in fact rather different from the effective paths. This difference
may not lead to serious bias in simple computations (such as the simplest two-input weighted
summation shown in their work), but as the computations become more complex, the
computational bias undoubtedly becomes larger. We also wish to point out that due to limitations
in their molecular design, they were unable to introduce null reporters in their system, which we
will explain in point 2 below.
We have made three key designs to enhance the robustness of the involved responses.
First, the toehold domain D was set to be 18 nucleotides long. Such a long length allows the
forward reaction (i.e., the formation of the PQT, PQ'T, or P'QT triplet) to be extremely
thermodynamically favorable, so that the conversion rate will be close to 100%, and thus the
entire forward reaction can be robustly repeated.
Second, a degenerate domain X and X are incorporated into the gate, and the P-strand
hybridizes only to domain B of the gate. Thus, domain X acts as an inhibitor, preventing leakage
between the P-strand and the gate in the absence of the Q-strand. This kind of leakage is very
common in strand replacement systems, and it would greatly impair the accuracy of the
simulation calculations.
Third, we set the longer T-strand as the output strand to eliminate the crosstalk between gates
and null gates. If we set the shorter O-strand as the output, which is commonly used in other
works 1, then the output O-strand in the gate should be fluorescently labeled, while the one in
the empty gate should be unlabeled. Since their sequences are identical, there will inevitably
be crosstalk between the O-strand and the gate, which will bias the signal and affect the
computational accuracy. Here, we set the longer strands as outputs, while the shorter O-strands
in both gates and empty gates are labeled with a bursting agent; thus, although crosstalk
between the O-strands and gates still exists, the fluorescence signals do not change as if the
crosstalk has been eliminated.
We wish to point out that none of the three strategies described above were developed by Genot
et al. in their Angew paper. Specifically, as we mentioned above, they did not design null
reporters because their outputs are shorter strands, and thus null reporters would crosstalk with
effective reporters; the negative effects of such crosstalk may outweigh the positive effects of
thermodynamically identical null reporters. Overall, Genot et al. did not develop any practical
strategy to improve the computational accuracy of their simulations, and it is no wonder that
their absolute computational bias is already close to 10% in the simplest two-input weighted
summation operation.
To summarize, in fact our FIRST is used for highly accurate positive weighted summation and
not for DNA neural networks, and we are not exaggerating on this point, but given that such a
description would still be controversial, we decided to change it to NEWEST.
REFERENCES:
Application to Matrix Multiplication and Weighted Sums. Angewandte Chemie
International Edition 52 (2013).
Q3b. The authors describe their system as the "first deep" DNA-based neural network - but what
does "deep" mean in this context? They demonstrate two layers, and their setup doesn't in fact
naturally allow for multiple layers. Instead, it is necessary to use a convoluted intervening step
involving magnetic beads. This is still an achievement, but the authors should be sure not to
mislead readers with the claims they present in the introduction and abstract.
Response: Thank you for raising your concerns regarding the depth of the convolutional
experiment. We would like to clarify that our convolutional process consists of three layers:
Convolutional Layer I, Convolutional Layer II, and a fully connected layer (see Figure 8E). In the
field of DNA neural networks, the understanding of convolutional depth is still evolving. If we
were to follow the standards proposed by some researchers2, our convolutional process would
actually achieve a depth of five layers (weighted summation + RELU + weighted summation +
RELU + weighted summation). However, according to the standard definition of neural
networks, the information processing following the weighted summation calculation, whether it
is simple addition and subtraction or complex RELU operations, is merged with the weighted
summation and considered as one layer. Therefore, our convolutional process is fully three
layers deep, whereas previous related literature only reported single-layer convolutional
processes. Given this comparison, we claim that our work represents the "first deep" DNA-
based neural network.

Q3d. The authors use the trans- version of their design to build "convolutional" neural networks.
However, these convolutional neural networks use a stride length equal to the kernel size, which
is not typically how convolutional neural networks operate (they would employ a smaller stride
length). ? This fact seems, to us, to be a fundamental result of the way the DNA-based system
works, rather than a simple choice that could be changed. The authors should therefore clarify
what their system is capable of.
Response: Thank you for your in-depth consideration of the convolutional computing structure.
In computer-based convolutional neural network models, the stride length is typically freely
adjustable, which helps enhance machine learning efficiency and performance. However, when
constructing DNA neural networks, the constraints of DNA reactions compel us to prioritize
maintaining simplicity in reaction quantity, DNA strand complexity, and structural design while
achieving computational functionality. We must acknowledge that implementing freely
configurable stride lengths in DNA neural networks remains highly challenging at present. After
comprehensive consideration, we therefore selected a specific stride length setting that allows
the convolutional kernel to precisely cover each input once. This design approach also
references published work on DNA convolutional neural networks2, which similarly utilized a
stride equivalent to the kernel size.

Q4. It is very hard to understand the behaviour that the authors expect from their reaction
networks. It would help a lot if, in the SI, the authors wrote down the ODEs that they believe
their various primitives should obey, and outline the assumptions under which the steady state
concentrations reach the desired values.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comments regarding the reaction process. We
acknowledge that your concerns may stem from an incomplete understanding of the
thermodynamic design underlying the experimental reaction process. The heating and annealing
process is not a simple reaction kinetics process occurring at room temperature, but rather a
rapid thermodynamic process. Therefore, we are unable to obtain the initial ODEs.
In the design of the gate strands, as previously addressed, we have elongated the X region,
making the thermodynamics extremely favorable. Once the kinetic barriers are removed through
heating and annealing, the strand displacement reaction rates in our system become very close
to 100% and remain stable. This represents the core innovation of our work, and all our
experimental results have validated our design and hypothesis.
Q5. The authors present the need to use the somewhat convoluted magnetic bead protocol in
order to demonstrate multi-layer operation as a result of the general existence of cross-talk in
DNA-based networks (lines 381-383). This seems to imply that it is the result of unitended
reactions between partially matched toeholds, for example. However, we believe that there is a
deeper issue in the specific context of the author's system, which is that their design inherently
requires *the same* strands to act as inputs at multiple layers of the system. If we are correct, this
is a challenge of a different type; it cannot be solved by making toeholds more orthogonal, etc.
Again, the authors need to be clearer about what their system can and cannot do.
Response: Thank you for your insightful question regarding the design of shared strands. We
hope Figure R5 can clarify how multi-layer CALCUL is designed and reacts without bead-
assisted conditions. When examining Figure R5 alongside Figure R1, it becomes evident that
simply extending the 3' end of the original O-strand with new domains to serve as input strands
for downstream reactions can fulfill multi-layer CALCUL operations.
In the cis-unit, the P-strand (domains A* and B) acts as the input strand, requiring the lower-
level input strand to adopt a similar structure. Thus, the original O-strand can be redesigned as
a P2-strand (domains X1, B, and C), where the B and C domains functionally serve as
downstream input for the new allosteric toehold strand displacement reaction. Here, the B
domain assumes the role of the original A* domain, while the C domain replaces the original B
domain. Similarly, in the trans-unit, the original O-strand can be redesigned as a Q2-strand
(domains X1, B, X2, and C), with the B, X2, and C domains acting as downstream inputs. The
B domain replaces the original D domain, the X2 domain substitutes the original X1 domain,
and the C domain takes over the function of the original A domain.
Kinetically, the single-stranded overhangs of the P2T-complex and Q2T-complex do not
directly react with downstream gate complexes. Leakage reactions only occur when the B
domain becomes transiently exposed due to strand breathing and the downstream input forms
a Q2P2 complex with the weight strand. Notably, the X1 domain significantly suppresses such
leakage.
Thermodynamically, the most significant change is that we can no longer employ immediate
heating-annealing after sample loading to accelerate reactions, as this would cause the terminal
gate strands to react uncontrollably without upstream signal regulation. Consequently, the
loading protocol must adopt traditional toehold DNA computing methods—pre-incubating gate
complexes and maintaining isothermal conditions. This will significantly prolong reaction time,
reduce computational accuracy, and impose stricter requirements on sequence design and
preliminary strand screening.
In summary, multi-layer CALCUL units remain computationally feasible without magnetic bead
assistance, eliminating the need for the same strands to act as inputs across multiple layers.
However, we must acknowledge that this design compromises the simplicity of strand reactions
and the stability and accuracy gained from heating-annealing protocols. These considerations
originally motivated our decision to introduce magnetic beads into the
multi-layer CALCUL system. We appreciate your question for prompting us to revisit and
systematically articulate these insights.
Figure R5. Molecular design of muti-layer CALCUL units without magnetic bead-assisted.

the intermediate weighted summation results but the final outputs after the complete ReLU
computation. Specifically, if we denote the weighted summation output as O, the final computed
value Y follows the ReLU equation: Y = O - b,if O ≥ b, and Y = 0, if O < b.
For the cis-CALCUL unit in Figure 7A, we set the threshold b at 0.20. Both the standard curve
and computational detection results underwent this ReLU operation. The standard curve values
of 0.00, 0.80, 1.80, and 3.80 were obtained by applying the ReLU function to the corresponding
weighted summation outputs (O) of 0.00, 1.00, 2.00, and 4.00, respectively. Similarly, the
weighted summation result of Pi and Qi was 3.00 in computational testing, which after ReLU
processing yielded the theoretical value of 2.80. The trans-CALCUL unit followed an identical
computational framework, with the only difference being the adjustment of the threshold b to
0.30.
These experimental standard curves and calculated values collectively provide a
comprehensive validation of the ReLU equation's computational results. Therefore, we did not
conduct additional experiments specifically targeting nonlinearity verification. We appreciate this
opportunity to clarify our methodology and hope this explanation adequately addresses your
concerns regarding Figure 7.
Q7. The final results in Fig. 8 are quite impressive, but they do show a fairly small differentiation
in many cases, and there is no clear distinction between output levels that correspond to positive
and negative results. It is unclear whether this is a failing of the DNA-based system, or of the
neural net that it is implementing. In Fig S5.1 and S7, the authors present charts showing the
"accuracy of trained neural network model(s)". We *think* (although we are not sure) that these are the in
silico models that are then implemented with DNA. They seem to have a high failure rate - is their
weakness what feeds through into the DNA system? Is the DNA system accurately reproducing the
flawed neural net? Moreover, if the in silico neural nets frequently make mistakes, how were
the 12 letters in Fig. 8 and the digits in Fig. 6 selected? Again, the authors need to be more
explicit about what they have successfully shown.
Response: Thank you for raising the question regarding the accuracy of the neural network
model. To maintain the relative simplicity of the experimental system, we employed a simplified,
shallow network that, while smaller in scale, incorporates all the functionalities we were able to
implement and those essential for a convolutional neural network (CNN). Specifically, the letter
recognition network shown in Figure 8 utilized only 23 parameters, while the digit recognition
network shown in Figure 6 used merely 16 parameters. For handwritten letter recognition tasks,
it is evident that a CNN with fewer than 30 parameters and at most two layers would not perform
well in terms of overall recognition accuracy. Typically, CNN models that achieve good
performance on the EMNIST dataset require thousands of parameters, which are currently
challenging to implement in our neural network framework.
However, our focus in this study is not on the recognition performance of the model itself, but
rather on whether our chemical system can precisely replicate the results obtained in silico. To
address this, we selected several examples that the in-silico model could correctly distinguish
(e.g., digits 8 and 9, and letters A and B) and conducted multiple chemical experiments. By
analyzing the results, we demonstrated that our chemical system is capable of accurately
reproducing the outcomes predicted by the model.
We hope this clarification addresses your concerns. Please let us know if further adjustments
are needed.

Q2. The basic gate design is a version of the associative toehold, introduced in 2011 by Xi
Chen. However, the authors call it "allosteric toehold" and do not cite this original paper.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your thoughtful question regarding our implementation of
allosteric toeholds. In our design, we incorporated allosteric toeholds to enable X/X allosteric
modification of the substrate (as illustrated in Figure R1). This strategic approach serves two
critical purposes: (1) the allosteric domain effectively prevents spurious interactions between
the P-strand and gate strand when the input strand Q is absent, and (2) it significantly mitigates
the accuracy reduction commonly observed in conventional strand displacement systems
(demonstrated in Figure 2 of the main text). For a more detailed discussion of the specific

Response: We sincerely appreciate your thorough and insightful comments regarding the
experimental principles. To ensure clarity, we will now provide a more detailed explanation of

"Notably, using the longer T-strand as output not only reduces crosstalk but also aids annealing,
as annealing can accelerate crosstalk, but our design prevents it from affecting the output
signal.The common approach of using the shorter O-strand as output is not suitable for
annealing and cannot achieve precise analogue computing."
In traditional DNA gate designs for molecular computing, the OT-complex conventionally uses
the short strand O as the output signal strand with a 3'-fluorophore modification, while the longer
strand T bearing a 5'-quencher typically remains uninvolved in signal output. Our CALCUL unit
design intentionally inverts this architecture by modifying the short O strand with a 3'-quencher
and the long T strand with a 5'-fluorophore. This strategic reversal allows us to introduce the O
strand in slight excess (specifically at 1.05 times the total concentration of T and T' strands, as
documented in the Supplementary Information), which provides multiple experimental
advantages without interfering with the primary reaction.
The modest excess of O strand effectively quenches fluorescence fluctuations arising from
concentration measurement inaccuracies and pipetting variations, thereby enhancing both the
reliability and precision of our computational results. Furthermore, our experimental
observations revealed that systems using short O strands as inputs exhibited significantly
degraded performance in both standard curve linearity and computational accuracy following
thermal annealing procedures. We attribute this phenomenon to the increased susceptibility of
short O strands to random dissociation and crosstalk during elevated temperature cycles - an
issue that is effectively circumvented by our alternative design employing the O strand as the
quenching component.
We have conducted systematic experiments to validate this design rationale, with the
corresponding methodology and results presented in Supplementary Information Figure
S3.2.1. We acknowledge that the original version of the manuscript did not discuss these
validation data in this particular section, an omission that may have created interpretative
challenges. To address this, we have incorporated these essential experimental findings in the
revised manuscript to ensure comprehensive understanding.

Q22. The authors should justify why image processing is useful in the context of DNA computing
(apart from just being a benchmark of computational power). Convolutional neural networks
were developed specifically to represent spatial features of images, but it is not clear from the
manuscript how this would be useful in molecular programming applications.
Response: Thank you for your insightful discussion on the specific applications of DNA
computing in image processing. DNA computing offers several unique advantages in this field:
Parallel Processing: DNA molecules can simultaneously perform a vast number of chemical
reactions, making them inherently suitable for parallel operations in image processing. For
example, the sliding of convolutional kernels and weight-sharing mechanisms in convolutional
neural networks (ConvNets) can be efficiently implemented through parallel DNA reactions.
Molecular-Scale Pattern Recognition: DNA molecules can mimic the pattern recognition
capabilities of biological neural networks through specific interactions. For instance, DNA strand
displacement reactions can simulate the multiplication and summation of weights between local
receptive fields of input images and convolutional kernels.
Fault Tolerance: DNA reactions exhibit inherent fault tolerance, enabling the processing of noisy
image data. Even when input images are similar, DNA circuits can accurately classify them.
Biocompatibility: The molecular nature of DNA computing allows it to interface directly with
biological systems. This feature holds great potential for future applications in biomedical image
analysis, such as molecular marker recognition in disease diagnosis.
Image processing not only serves as a testbed for validating DNA computing capabilities but
also highlights its unique advantages. The parallelism, molecular-level analog capabilities, noise
resistance, and biocompatibility of DNA computing make it promising for tasks such as pattern
recognition and medical image analysis, paving the way for the development of future molecular
intelligent systems.
Many related studies are currently exploring this field (e.g., DNA-based biocomputing circuits
for sensing and processing biomolecular information, and DNA circuits for real-time computing
and control inside living cells). Building on these efforts, we continue to develop new
foundational tools and aim to demonstrate their functionality in image recognition.
We hope this explanation clarifies the potential applications of DNA computing in image
processing. Please let us know if further details are needed.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, Liu, et al. demonstrate the capabilities of a DNA convolutional neural network
in which inputs, weights and outputs are both continuous values. The unique molecular design
of the cis- and trans- CALCUL computing units ensures operational stability and accuracy,
allowing high-parallelism convolutional operations to be performed in a single
reaction tube. This offers invaluable guidance for enhancing the scalability and computational
accuracy of DNA neural networks in the future. Eventually, they successfully constructed a deep
DNA neural network containing convolutional layers and fully connected layers to recognize
144-pixel images.
The paper is scientifically accurate and the authors present their findings with critical and
effective analysis. The methods and the statistical analysis are clearly described. The figures
and tables are informative. I suggest accepting this manuscript after they address the following
concerns.
Comments
Q1.For terms that may be unfamiliar to non-professional readers, such as “ConvNet”, it is
recommended to provide a brief explanation when they first appear to improve the readability
of the paper.
Response: Thank you for your suggestion. We have provided more detailed explanations for
the technical terms that appear for the first time in the original text.
Q2. The article proposes the CALCUL computing unit based on the allosteric-toehold domain,
but the explanation of its operational principles and how it enhances computational stability and
accuracy is insufficient. It would be beneficial if the authors could provide a more comprehensive
description of the CALCUL unit's strand reaction process, specifically addressing how continuity
and accuracy are maintained in the inputs, weights, and outputs. Additionally, it is important to
clearly illustrate the role of allosteric-toehold domain design in this process.
Response: We sincerely appreciate both Reviewer 1 and Reviewer 2 for raising this important
question regarding computational accuracy. As detailed in our response to Reviewer 1 (Q2c,
Q3a and Q14) and systematically illustrated in Figure R1 and Figure 2 of the main text, we
have implemented multiple design strategies to ensure high precision. For clarity, we summarize
the key points here:
We attribute the significant improvement in computational precision to three design features and
one reaction advantage:
1. Design Features
(1) Optimized Toehold Domain
An 18-nt toehold domain (D) was implemented to maximize forward reaction efficiency,
achieving near-complete conversion and high reproducibility.
(2) Leakage Prevention
The *X/X** allosteric domain in the gate complex eliminates spurious interactions between the
P-strand and gate in the absence of the Q-strand, addressing a key accuracy-limiting factor in
strand displacement systems.
(3) Crosstalk Mitigation
Designating the longer T-strand as the output strand ensures fluorescence signal stability
mitigate potential crosstalk between functional and void gates, preserving computational
fidelity.
2. Reaction Advantage
Thermal Annealing Compatibility
The allosteric toehold strand displacement reaction is thermodynamically irreversible, enabling
our system to achieve rapid equilibrium through thermal annealing. By mixing all DNA strands
in a single step and applying thermal annealing, the reaction reaches completion within minutes
while eliminating kinetic traps - a process that simultaneously maintains computational accuracy
and stability.
These synergistic features collectively enable the demonstrated high-precision performance
(The validation data are shown in Figure 4D).
Additionally, in response to Reviewer 2 s emphasis on achieving continuous computational
values, we would like to supplement the explanation with Figure 1 in the main text. The core
principle enabling continuous-value multiplication operation in our study relies on mixing
effective and ineffective weight strands, allowing input strands to partition into different reaction
pathways according to the concentration ratios of weight strands. Here, the effective pathway
generates fluorescent signal output, while the ineffective pathway merely consumes substrate
without producing output (in multi-layer neural network construction, fluorescent signals are
replaced by domain signals transmitted through biotin modification and magnetic bead
separation).
In cis-CALCUL units, pathway partitioning is achieved through combinations of:
Effective components: Q strands with OT-complex gates
Ineffective components: Q strands with OT -complex gates
These pathways feature distinct structural characteristics:
Effective pathway: Shares identical D/D* domains with 5 -fluorophore modification on T-strand
Ineffective pathway: Shares identical D /D * domains without 5 -end modification
For trans-CALCUL units, pathway partitioning requires only:
Effective P strands (unmodified 3 end)
Ineffective P strands (3 -quencher modification)
Despite their identical DNA sequences, P and P strands achieve functional differentiation solely
through this terminal modification, while sharing the same OT-complex.
As demonstrated in Figure 1, stable parallel reactions producing fixed product ratios emerge
when specific concentrations of P, Q, O, and T strands are introduced. This reaction framework
serves as the foundation for our weighted summation computational units.
Fig. 1. The working principles of the cis-CALCUL and trans-CALCUL units. A) Schematic
illustration of the weighted summation operation of the cis-CALCUL unit. Multiplexed CAT
reactions are undergoing within one tube, realizing “real” weighted summation operation with
the inputs, weights and outputs all being continuous and accurate values. B) Schematic
illustration of the weighted summation operation of the trans-CALCUL unit. Similarly, based on
Multiplexed CAT reactions, but with different roles played by the domains compared to cis-
CALCUL units, which helps it to be more suitable for convolution operations.
